ut.title: Ultrasonic Testing & UT Thickness Inspection | Mobile, AL
ut.description: On-site ultrasonic thickness testing and UT weld inspection in Mobile, Alabama: shipyard steel, port structures and chemical piping. Request a quote today.
ut.h1: Ultrasonic Testing (UT) Inspection in Mobile, Alabama
ut.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II ultrasonic technicians to sites in Mobile, Alabama for thickness surveys on piping, vessels and tanks, and for angle-beam examination of welds in structural and pressure steel. The work covers shipyard and fabrication steel, chemical and paper-mill piping, port equipment and storage tanks. Send us the asset list, drawings and the code your owner or inspector works to, and request a UT inspection quote for Mobile.

Where ultrasonic inspection earns its keep in Mobile

Mobile is Alabama's only seaport, and its industry is built around the water. Steel and aluminum ships are built and repaired on the river, bulk and container cargo moves across the docks, and chemical, paper and steel producers sit along the corridor that feeds the port. Each of those settings leaves steel that thins, cracks or hides weld defects, and ultrasonic testing is the usual way to measure it from one side without cutting anything open.

On the industrial side the typical targets are carbon steel process piping carrying caustic, acid, brine or hydrocarbon service; heat exchanger shells; pressure vessels and surge drums; and atmospheric storage tanks. Paper and wood-products mills add steam piping, digester and boiler components, and long runs of condensate line where erosion and under-insulation corrosion are routine. Along the waterfront, UT thickness readings are taken on sheet pile and bulkhead steel, crane runway girders, and the legs and pins of heavy lifting equipment.

Fabrication shops serving the shipbuilding and offshore trades need weld examination more than corrosion mapping. A shop building structural modules or pressure skids may be asked to prove that groove welds are free of lack of fusion before paint, and that is where shear-wave work comes in. Our national ultrasonic testing service page describes the general scope; this page covers how it applies in Mobile.

What UT measures, and what it cannot see

A contact transducer sends a short pulse of sound into the steel and the instrument displays the returning echoes against time. For thickness, the time between the front surface and the back-wall echo, multiplied by the sound velocity for that material, gives wall thickness. For welds, an angled shear wave travels through the fusion zone and reflects from planar flaws such as lack of fusion, cracks and incomplete penetration, which show on the screen as echoes between the entry point and the back wall.

The method has real limits that matter on Gulf Coast steel. Heavy scale, flaking paint and rough corrosion pits scatter sound and can hide a loss of wall or give a false reading, so surface preparation is part of the job. Thick coatings on ship plating and tank shells can be measured through only when the procedure has been proven on a matching sample. Cast and coarse-grained material, such as some austenitic stainless weld metal, attenuates the beam and may need a different technique or a different method altogether. Laminations in plate can sit directly under a weld and block the beam, so scanning for them before weld work is routine on thick plate.

Ultrasonic testing also does not tell you the cause of a flaw. A reflector is sized, located and compared with the acceptance rules; an engineer or the owner's authorized inspector decides what happens next. Where a surface-breaking crack is suspected, an MT or PT check from our magnetic particle and penetrant pages is often the quick confirmation.

Codes and acceptance criteria used for Mobile work

The code decides how the examination is done and what is rejected. For shop and field welds in process piping, ASME B31.3 sets the examination extent and the acceptance criteria in Table 341.3.2, and ultrasonic technique follows ASME Section V, Article 4 for welds and Article 5 for materials. Pressure vessel welds built to ASME Section VIII Division 1 use Mandatory Appendix 12 for ultrasonic examination of welds. Structural steel work follows AWS D1.1, which has its own ultrasonic acceptance rules for groove welds, and ASTM E164 and E114 cover the contact technique and equipment checks.

Thickness readings are governed by ASME Section V Article 5 and by ASTM E797, the practice for contact pulse-echo thickness measurement. In-service inspection of vessels, piping and tanks falls under API 510, API 570 and API 653, where the owner's authorized inspector is responsible for the inspection program. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic work and reports the data, such as thickness at each condition monitoring location, and does not act as that authorized inspector.

Alabama also regulates pressure equipment. The Alabama Department of Workforce runs the boiler and pressure vessel inspection program under the Alabama Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act, with regular inspections and operating certificates for equipment that the act covers. Our thickness records can support the owner's inspector when a vessel is due. Owners should confirm which of their equipment is covered and who holds the commission for it.

How the ultrasonic work is performed

For corrosion and erosion surveys, the technician lays out a grid or a set of condition monitoring locations, marks them so the same spots can be read next time, and cleans each point down to bright metal. A dual-element probe is the normal choice on corroded surfaces because its separate transmit and receive crystals handle rough back walls better than a single-element probe. The instrument is calibrated on a step block of the same alloy before the work, rechecked during it, and verified again at the end.

A-scan display is used rather than reading a bare number off a digital gauge. Watching the waveform lets the technician see a doubled echo on thin wall, a laminar reflector or a pitted back wall that a numeric readout would misreport. Hot surfaces need a high-temperature probe and couplant, and the reading is corrected for the temperature effect on velocity. On insulated lines, the insulation is stripped at the test points by the owner's crew and replaced afterward.

For weld examination, angle-beam probes in the 45, 60 and 70 degree range are chosen for the joint geometry and wall thickness. A reference level is built from the code's calibration block, usually with side-drilled holes, and the weld is scanned from both sides where access allows, with the weld crown ground flush or the scan surface prepared beside it. Indications above the recording threshold are located, measured in length and compared with the acceptance table. A short sketch of each rejectable indication goes into the report.

Who performs and reviews the work

Atlantis technicians are qualified under the company written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician sets up and calibrates the instrument, performs the examination and interprets the results against the code. The written procedure is approved, and each report reviewed, by an ASNT Level III before it reaches you. Reports are reviewed by Anoop Rayavarapu, who holds ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

Atlantis has no office in Mobile. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, and we plan the visit around your access dates rather than a standing local presence. Certification of any individual belongs to the employer under SNT-TC-1A, so your own contractor's technicians hold their own employer's certificate. If you want procedures or a written practice reviewed before a job starts, the Level III consulting page explains that service.

Atlantis is certified to ISO 9001 and ISO 14001, and that covers how the company controls documents, equipment and records. The qualification of individual technicians remains a separate matter handled under the written practice.

What an ultrasonic report from Atlantis contains

Each report identifies the component, line number or tank, drawing reference and the code that governs the job. It lists the procedure and revision used, the instrument, probes and calibration blocks with their serial numbers, the couplant and the calibration checks. The technician's name and certification level appear on every sheet, and the Level III review is recorded.

For thickness work you receive a thickness grid or a table by condition monitoring location, with the nominal wall, the minimum required wall if the owner provides it, the readings and the date. Locations that fall below the owner's limit are flagged for the engineer. For welds, the report lists each recordable indication by position along the weld, depth, length and amplitude, and states accept or reject against the named criteria. Photographs and sketches of the scan setup are included where useful, so a later crew can repeat the examination in the same way.

Planning a UT job in Mobile

Mobile summers are hot and humid, and steel left in the sun can be too hot to touch. That affects couplant choice, probe wear and how long a technician can work in the field before a break. Winters are mild but occasionally reach freezing, and thickness readings on cold steel need the calibration block at the same temperature as the part. Hurricane season, from June through November, can close ports and shipyards with little notice, so schedules near the water carry some weather contingency.

Shipyard and port work usually involves badging, safety orientation, hot-work and confined-space rules, and sometimes escort requirements. Send those details early. Chemical and paper plants have their own turnaround windows, and the right time to read thickness on a line is while it is empty and accessible for cleaning. Highway and rail access into the Mobile area is good, which keeps mobilization simple for visiting crews, and we confirm lodging and the start date once the scope is agreed.

A note on ships: thickness readings on vessel plating taken by Atlantis are for the owner's own maintenance decisions. Atlantis does not hold class-society approval for thickness measurement. Gauging that has to be credited to a class survey must be done by a firm approved by that vessel's classification society.

UT, MT or PT for your Mobile job

Choose ultrasonic testing when the question is how much steel remains or whether a weld is sound all the way through. Choose magnetic particle inspection when you need to find surface and near-surface cracks on carbon steel, such as at the toe of a fillet weld on a crane pedestal, since MT is fast and sensitive there. Choose liquid penetrant testing for surface-breaking flaws on stainless steel, aluminum hull plate or nickel alloys, where magnetic methods do not work.

Many jobs use two methods together. A pressure vessel weld repair, for example, may need PT on the ground-out cavity, UT on the finished weld and a final thickness check. The three Mobile pages, together with the Alabama inspection services page, show how the methods split. The ultrasonic testing guide gives more background on probe selection and calibration.

Training your own UT technicians

If your company wants its own staff qualified, the route starts with training hours and documented experience under your written practice. We offer UT Level 1 training and UT Level 2 training, with theory delivered online and hands-on practice at your facility. The ultrasonic testing simulator lets trainees practice scanning before they touch real equipment. Our Mobile training page explains how courses are delivered for local employers, and the SNT-TC-1A eligibility checker shows the hours required for each level.

faq.q: What does ultrasonic thickness testing cost to arrange in Mobile, Alabama?
faq.a: The effort depends on how many condition monitoring locations you have, the access and surface preparation needed, and the travel for the crew. Send the asset list and drawings through the quote link and we will scope the job against your code and inspector.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing be done on painted or coated steel in Mobile?
faq.a: Often yes, but the coating must be sound and the procedure proven on a sample with the same coating. Loose paint, scale and heavy fouling are removed first, because they scatter sound and can hide real wall loss.

faq.q: Does Atlantis inspect ship hulls in Mobile with UT?
faq.a: Atlantis can take ultrasonic thickness readings on vessel plating for the owner's own maintenance decisions. It has no class-society approval for thickness measurement, so readings that must be credited to a class survey need a class-approved firm.

faq.q: Which code governs UT weld inspection on pressure piping near Mobile?
faq.a: Process piping is normally examined to ASME B31.3 with technique from ASME Section V Article 4. Pressure vessels use ASME Section VIII Division 1, Appendix 12, and structural steel uses AWS D1.1. Your engineer names the governing code.

faq.q: Do you replace the owner's API authorized inspector?
faq.a: No. Under API 510, API 570 and API 653 the owner's authorized inspector remains responsible for the inspection program. Atlantis performs the ultrasonic examination and supplies the thickness and indication data for that inspector to evaluate.

faq.q: How are Atlantis technicians qualified for UT?
faq.a: Technicians are qualified under the company written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II performs and interprets the examination, and an ASNT Level III approves the procedure and reviews the report before it is issued.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis crew stationed in Mobile?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Mobile. Technicians travel to your site for the agreed scope, and we coordinate access dates, badging and safety orientation with your plant or yard before mobilizing.

faq.q: Can ultrasonic testing find surface cracks on a weld?
faq.a: UT can detect cracks that reflect the beam, but surface-breaking cracks near the toe are usually confirmed faster with magnetic particle testing on carbon steel or penetrant testing on non-magnetic metals, so many welds receive both.

faq.q: How should I prepare a line or vessel for UT in Mobile?
faq.a: Make the test points accessible, remove insulation at those spots, clean each location to bright metal, and tell us the operating temperature. Hot lines need high-temperature probes and couplant, and sometimes a shutdown.

mt.title: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MPI) in Mobile, AL | MT
mt.description: Magnetic particle inspection and mag particle testing for welds, crane steel and plant equipment in Mobile, Alabama. Send your scope for a quote today.
mt.h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection (MT) in Mobile, Alabama
mt.html:
Atlantis NDT sends Level II magnetic particle technicians to Mobile, Alabama to check carbon and low-alloy steel for surface and near-surface cracks. Typical scopes are weld toes on structural steel and crane pedestals, repaired areas on pressure equipment, lifting gear, fabrication welds and heavy rolling-stock or port machinery. Tell us the component, the code and the surface condition, then request an MT inspection quote for Mobile.

Where magnetic particle testing is used around Mobile

Mobile combines shipbuilding, steel production, chemical plants, paper mills and a busy port, and nearly all of that equipment is ferromagnetic steel. That is the ideal case for MT. Fabricators building hull sections, deck structures and equipment foundations use it to check fillet and groove welds for toe cracks and arc strikes. Repair yards grind out suspected cracks and use MT to prove the cavity is clean before welding resumes.

At the docks, heavy cargo handling concentrates stress in a few places. Crane booms, slewing rings, pedestal welds, spreader bars, shackles, hooks and padeyes all see cyclic loading, and fatigue cracks start at welds and sharp changes of section. A magnetic particle check at those points during a planned inspection can find cracks while they are still short. Industrial plants add pressure vessel nozzle welds, support lugs, structural pipe racks, and the attachment welds on tanks and heat exchangers.

Steel mills and metal fabricators around the area also run rotating and rolling equipment where shafts, rolls and gear teeth are examined for service cracks. For the broader national scope see our magnetic particle testing service page; this page explains how the method fits Mobile jobs.

What MT finds and what it misses

Magnetic particle inspection works by magnetizing the part, so that any surface or slightly subsurface discontinuity distorts the magnetic field and attracts fine ferromagnetic particles. The particles gather over the flaw and form a visible line. Because the method depends on magnetism, it applies only to ferromagnetic material such as carbon steel and low-alloy steel. It does not work on austenitic stainless steel, aluminum, copper or most nickel alloys, which are common in marine and chemical settings. Those parts need liquid penetrant testing instead.

The method is strongest on flaws that lie across the magnetic field. A crack running parallel to the field lines may produce no indication at all, which is why the part is magnetized in two directions. Depth sensitivity falls quickly below the surface, so MT is a surface and near-surface method; it will not size a deep embedded flaw. Thick paint, weld spatter and rust weaken indications, and excessive coating may require removal. Non-relevant indications can appear at section changes or where two metals meet, and the technician has to judge them correctly.

When the question is wall loss or buried weld flaws, ultrasonic testing is the right tool; the Mobile UT page covers that.

Codes and acceptance criteria for MT in Mobile

The governing code names the technique and the rejection limits. ASME Section V, Article 7 gives the requirements for the magnetic particle method, and ASTM E709 and E1444 are the reference guide and practice. ASME B31.3 requires magnetic particle examination under paragraph 344.3 with acceptance in Table 341.3.2, and ASME Section VIII Division 1 uses Mandatory Appendix 6 for MT methods and acceptance on pressure vessels.

Structural welds and many shipyard fabrications are checked to AWS D1.1, which describes magnetic particle examination of welds and lists the surface discontinuity limits. Many shipbuilding specifications add their own contract requirements, so your drawings and specification package control the job. In-service pressure equipment under API 510, API 570 or API 653 stays under the owner's authorized inspector, and Atlantis supplies the examination findings for that person.

The Alabama Department of Workforce administers the state boiler and pressure vessel program under the Alabama Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act, which calls for regular inspections and operating certificates on covered equipment. When a repair has been made to a covered vessel, MT records of the repaired weld area can form part of the owner's file. Confirm with your inspector which repairs need documentation before work starts.

How magnetic particle inspection is done

Field work is usually done with an electromagnetic yoke, which lets the technician magnetize a small region at a time, or with prods for heavier sections where AC contact current is permitted. ASME Section V sets a minimum lifting force for yokes, so the yoke is checked against a test weight at the maximum pole spacing before use. Each area is examined with the field in two roughly perpendicular directions, so cracks in any orientation are caught.

Particles may be dry powder, which suits rough welds and heated surfaces, or a wet suspension. Wet fluorescent particles are more sensitive and are examined under ultraviolet light in a darkened area, with the light intensity checked before examining. Where a contrast paint background is applied, visible particles in a contrasting color are used under white light. Field indicators, such as a pie gauge or a shim, confirm that the field strength is adequate for the particular surface and technique.

After examination, indications are marked, photographed when needed, and compared with the acceptance table. If residual magnetism could affect later welding, machining or an instrument, the part is demagnetized and checked with a gauss meter. Surfaces are then cleaned of particles. Heavy mill scale and slag on welds must be removed first, because a crack hidden under slag will not produce a clear indication.

Surface condition and typical indications on Mobile steel

Weld toe cracks, lack of sidewall fusion that reaches the surface, arc strikes, laps and grinding cracks are the indications most often found on shipyard and structural steel. Heat-affected zones that have been rapidly cooled can develop hydrogen cracks, which sometimes appear hours or days after welding, so a hold period before examination may be written into the procedure. Cyclic loading at the dock produces fatigue cracks that start at notches and often grow in a direction that the two-direction technique is designed to catch.

Coastal air and splash zones leave salt, rust and marine growth on steel. Preparation is usually by wire brushing, grinding or light blasting until the metal is clean and dry enough for the particles to move freely. Oil and grease are removed with a solvent, because they cause particles to clump and give false patterns. Rough weld profiles can trap particles, so the technician looks at whether an indication is relevant, caused by geometry, or a true discontinuity before it is recorded. Where doubt remains, the area is cleaned, re-magnetized and re-examined, and a second method may be used to confirm.

Qualification and review

MT is performed by Atlantis technicians qualified under the company written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. The Level II technician performs the examination, interprets the indications and records them. An ASNT Level III approves the technique sheet and signs off on the report. Anoop Rayavarapu is the company's Level III, qualified in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

Mobile has no Atlantis premises. Crews are mobilized to your shipyard, plant or fabrication shop for the agreed scope, and the work is organized around your site access rather than a standing presence nearby. Under SNT-TC-1A each employer certifies its own personnel, so any technician you employ directly is certified by your company. Procedure help and written practice work are offered through our written practice development service.

What the MT report includes

A magnetic particle report identifies the component, location, drawing number and the governing code. It records the technique used, whether yoke or prods, the particle type and color, the lighting levels and the field direction. Equipment details such as the yoke's serial number and the date of its last lifting-force check are listed, along with the technician's name and level.

Every indication is described by location, length and orientation, and the report states whether it is accepted or rejected against the named criteria. A sketch or a photograph shows where each indication lies. If a weld was dressed and re-examined after a repair, both results appear so the record shows what was found and what was removed. Level III review is recorded on the document before it reaches you.

Planning an MT job in Mobile

Hot Gulf Coast summers raise steel temperatures well above comfortable levels, and wet particle suspensions behave differently on hot metal, so dry particles or a heat-tolerant technique may be specified. In the cool season, cold steel is rarely a problem in Mobile, though occasional freezes require the part and materials to be within the procedure's temperature range. Humidity and sea air speed up rusting after cleaning, so surfaces are examined soon after preparation.

Fluorescent inspection needs darkness. Outdoors in daylight, that means a portable dark enclosure or a tent; inside a hull block or a vessel, it is easier. Plan for lighting, power for the yoke and a place to stage equipment. Shipyards and port terminals typically require safety orientation and badging before crews enter, and plants require hot-work or confined-space permits when examining inside vessels. Hurricane season can interrupt work near the water, so leave scheduling room.

When the work is on a ship, our readings and findings are for the owner's own decisions. Atlantis holds no class-society approval for ship thickness measurement, and class-credited surveys require firms approved by the vessel's society.

MT, PT or UT in Mobile

For carbon steel welds that need a fast check for surface cracks, magnetic particle inspection is usually the first choice because it is quick, sensitive and shows the flaw directly on the surface. If the part is stainless steel, aluminum or a non-ferrous alloy, use liquid penetrant testing. If you need to know whether a flaw extends below the surface or how much metal remains, use ultrasonic testing.

The MT versus PT comparison goes into more detail. For work covering all of Alabama, see the Alabama inspection services page. A few jobs benefit from combining methods, for example PT on a stainless pipe weld and MT on its carbon steel support attachments in the same shutdown.

Training MT technicians in your company

Companies that want their own people qualified start with formal instruction, then practical hours on real parts, under their written practice. We provide MT Level 1 training and MT Level 2 training, and the Mobile training page explains how courses reach local employers. The complete MT guide is a good starting read for new technicians, and the practice tests help check progress.

faq.q: Which materials can magnetic particle inspection be used on in Mobile?
faq.a: MT works only on ferromagnetic materials such as carbon and low-alloy steel. Austenitic stainless steel, aluminum and copper alloys are not magnetic, so those parts are examined with liquid penetrant testing instead.

faq.q: What can MT find on a crane or heavy lifting structure?
faq.a: It finds surface and slightly subsurface cracks, most often fatigue cracks at weld toes, pins, pedestals and changes of section. It is not suited to measuring remaining wall thickness, which is a job for ultrasonic testing.

faq.q: Is fluorescent or visible particle testing used on Mobile jobs?
faq.a: Both are used. Fluorescent wet particles give higher sensitivity but need a dark area and ultraviolet light. Visible dry or wet particles with contrast paint work better outdoors or on rough welds. Your code and procedure decide.

faq.q: Which codes govern magnetic particle inspection of welds?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 7 gives the method, with acceptance from the construction code, for example ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2, Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 6 or AWS D1.1. Your engineer or specification names the one that applies.

faq.q: Does Atlantis perform magnetic particle testing on ships?
faq.a: Atlantis can examine welds and structures on a vessel for the owner's own decisions. It holds no class-society approval, so examinations that must be credited to a class survey need a firm approved by that society.

faq.q: Is an Atlantis crew stationed in Mobile?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Mobile. Technicians are mobilized to your site for the agreed scope, and we coordinate site access, orientation and safety paperwork with you ahead of the job.

faq.q: Why is demagnetizing needed after MT?
faq.a: Residual magnetism can pull steel chips to a surface, disturb arc direction during welding, or interfere with instruments and machining. When it could matter, the part is demagnetized and checked with a field meter before it is released.

faq.q: Can MT be done on painted steel in Mobile?
faq.a: Thin, tight coatings may be acceptable if the procedure has shown that indications still form, but thick or flaking paint lowers sensitivity. The coating is often removed at the examination area, and the report notes what was done.

faq.q: What should I send to get an MT quote for a Mobile site?
faq.a: Send the component list or drawings, the governing code, surface condition, access notes, temperature, and any site orientation requirements. With that we can define the technique and the scope for the quotation.

pt.title: Dye Penetrant Inspection (PT) in Mobile, Alabama
pt.description: Liquid penetrant testing and dye penetrant inspection for stainless, aluminum and steel welds in Mobile, Alabama shipyards and plants. Request a quote.
pt.h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing (PT) in Mobile, Alabama
pt.html:
Atlantis NDT mobilizes Level II technicians to Mobile, Alabama for dye penetrant inspection of welds and machined parts in stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and carbon steel. The method suits aluminum ship structure, stainless chemical piping, repair cavities and fabricated assemblies, because it needs no magnetism and no power. Send the material, the code and the surface condition, then request a PT inspection quote for Mobile.

Why penetrant testing matters in Mobile

Mobile builds and repairs vessels in aluminum as well as steel, and aluminum cannot be examined with magnetic particles. Local chemical plants run stainless and alloy piping that is equally non-magnetic. Steel producers in the region work with stainless grades too. For all of these materials, liquid penetrant is the standard way to find cracks that reach the surface, and it is just as useful on carbon steel when magnetism is impractical, such as on small parts or complex shapes.

Aluminum fabrication is a good illustration. Weld crater cracks, porosity breaking the surface, and toe cracks are common defects in aluminum plate and extrusions, and PT shows them without damaging the surface. Marine hardware, such as fittings, bracket welds, hatches, handrail posts and engine-room foundations, is routinely checked this way. In the process plants, PT is used on stainless nozzle welds, thermowell attachments, valve bodies, pump casings and the weld overlay areas of vessels.

Port and industrial machinery includes castings and forgings in stainless or alloy grades where the question is simply whether a surface crack exists. The national penetrant testing service page describes the general method; below is how it applies to Mobile.

What penetrant testing detects and where it stops

Liquid penetrant testing finds only flaws that are open to the surface. The liquid enters a crack, lap, pore or seam by capillary action, the excess is removed, and a developer draws the trapped liquid back out so that the flaw appears as a colored line or dot. It works on any non-porous material, ferrous or not, which is its main advantage.

Its limits are equally important. A flaw that does not reach the surface is invisible to PT, however large it is. Surfaces that have been peened, shot blasted, ground smooth or machined heavily can smear metal across a crack mouth and close it, so a light etch is sometimes required before inspection. Porous materials, rough surfaces and heavily contaminated parts absorb or hold penetrant and produce a confusing background. Paint, oil, scale and weld flux all block the penetrant from entering and must be removed first.

For anything below the surface, or for wall thinning, ultrasonic testing is needed instead, and our Mobile UT page explains that route. On carbon steel where speed is wanted, magnetic particle inspection is often quicker.

Codes and acceptance criteria for PT in Mobile

ASME Section V, Article 6 sets the requirements for liquid penetrant examination, and ASTM E165 is the general industry practice. Acceptance criteria come from the construction code: ASME B31.3 requires penetrant examination under paragraph 344.4 with limits in Table 341.3.2, and ASME Section VIII Division 1 uses Mandatory Appendix 8 for penetrant methods and acceptance. AWS D1.1 permits penetrant examination of welds in structural steel, and many shipbuilding or equipment specifications add their own acceptance rules.

Sulfur and halogen content matters on stainless steel and nickel alloys, because certain contaminants can attack those materials. Procedures for such work specify penetrant materials with low chlorine, fluorine and sulfur content, and the batch certifications are kept with the job records. For in-service vessels and piping, the owner's authorized inspector under API 510 or API 570 remains responsible; Atlantis reports the examination results for that inspector to evaluate.

The Alabama Department of Workforce runs the state boiler and pressure vessel program under the Alabama Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety Act. Where a repair weld on a covered vessel was checked by PT, the record may be needed in the owner's file. It is worth asking your inspector early which documents the state and the owner require.

How a penetrant examination is carried out

The steps are the same on every job, and each one has a minimum time or condition in the procedure. First the surface is cleaned and dried, with solvents or mechanical cleaning, until there is no oil, paint, scale or flux in the way. Penetrant is applied by spray, brush or immersion and left on the surface for the dwell time written in the procedure, which depends on the material, the type of flaw expected and the temperature.

The excess penetrant is then removed. Solvent-removable penetrants are wiped with lint-free cloth, then lightly dampened cloth, and the surface is never flooded, since that can wash penetrant out of a flaw. Water-washable and post-emulsifiable systems are used in shops. Developer is applied as a thin, even layer, normally a non-aqueous spray in field work, and the part is examined after the development time. Visible dye penetrants are read under good white light, while fluorescent penetrants are examined under ultraviolet light in a darkened area.

After the examination the surface is cleaned again so that penetrant residues do not interfere with welding, coating or service. On stainless and alloy materials, a final cleaning step helps remove any remaining materials. Test blocks or comparators are used to verify that the system is performing as expected, particularly when conditions are unusual.

Temperature, humidity and surface prep in Mobile

ASME Section V Article 6 sets the standard temperature range for the part and the penetrant materials as 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit, which is 5 to 52 degrees Celsius. Beyond those limits the procedure has to be demonstrated at the actual temperature. In Mobile this limit is more likely to be exceeded in summer than winter, since steel baking in direct sun can exceed the upper limit while the air feels merely hot. Technicians measure part temperature with a contact or surface thermometer, and shade or cooling may be necessary.

High humidity affects drying time after cleaning and can leave moisture in tight cracks, which blocks penetrant entry. Plan extra time for drying, and avoid examination in rain or when dew is forming on the metal. Salt air leaves chloride on exposed surfaces, so a thorough clean is part of the preparation for stainless and aluminum work, and a final clean afterward removes residues that could otherwise promote corrosion.

Choosing the penetrant system for the job

Visible dye penetrant is the usual field choice because it needs only good white light and no darkened area, and it gives a red indication against a white developer background. Fluorescent penetrant is more sensitive to fine, tight cracks and is favored on critical aluminum and alloy components, but it requires a dark space and an ultraviolet lamp whose intensity is verified. The penetrant is also classed by how the excess is removed: solvent-removable for portable work, water-washable for shop parts, and post-emulsifiable where the highest sensitivity is needed.

Sensitivity levels matter when the part has a rough finish, because a more sensitive penetrant also leaves more background that has to be washed away. A weld in as-welded condition, with ripples and spatter, may call for a different system than a machined shaft. Our Level III writes or approves the procedure so that the system matches the surface and the acceptance standard. A known-defect comparator block is used to confirm that the chosen system actually reveals cracks of the size the code cares about.

Who performs PT and who reviews it

Atlantis technicians are qualified under the company written practice, which follows ASNT SNT-TC-1A. A Level II technician performs the examination, interprets indications and records results. The procedure is approved and the report reviewed by an ASNT Level III, and that role belongs to Anoop Rayavarapu, ASNT NDT Level III in UT, RT, MT, PT and VT.

The company has no office in Mobile, and crews are mobilized to the site for the agreed scope. Employers certify their own personnel under SNT-TC-1A, so a client wanting its own staff certified would do so through its own written practice, which we can help to develop through the Level III consulting service. The company holds ISO 9001 and ISO 14001 certificates that cover its management systems.

What the PT report contains

The report names the component, drawing, material and code. It lists the procedure and revision, the penetrant type and method (visible or fluorescent, and how the excess was removed), the product brand and batch numbers, the dwell and development times, and the part temperature. Lighting levels are recorded for visible and ultraviolet examinations.

Each indication is described by its location, shape and size, and the report states accepted or rejected against the criteria in the code. Photographs of rejectable indications are attached where possible, and a sketch shows their position. Cleaning steps and any repair-and-reexamination sequence are recorded so that the file shows the history of the part.

Planning a PT job in Mobile

Marine and chemical sites place restrictions on solvents and sprays. Confined spaces such as tanks, void spaces and the insides of hull sections need ventilation and a permit, and flammable penetrant cleaners are not welcome near hot work. Tell us early what the site allows, and we can choose water-washable or solvent-removable materials accordingly. Aluminum ship structure may also have coatings applied soon after fabrication, so examination is scheduled before painting.

Shipyards and port terminals require badging and safety orientation, and industrial plants may restrict visitors during turnarounds. Hurricane season, from June to November, can close yards at short notice. We coordinate dates around such events. Work on vessels is for the owner's own decisions: Atlantis does not hold class-society approval for ship thickness measurement, and class-credited gauging needs a class-approved firm.

PT, MT or UT for your Mobile job

Choose penetrant testing for stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys and any other non-magnetic metal, for small or irregular parts, and when you only need to know whether a surface crack exists. Choose magnetic particle inspection for carbon steel where speed matters. Choose ultrasonic testing when a flaw may lie below the surface or when wall loss is the question.

The comparison of MT and PT and the Article 6 explanation give more detail, and the Alabama inspection page shows how services fit across the state.

Training penetrant technicians

If your staff are to perform PT themselves, they need classroom instruction and documented practice. We offer PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training, with the penetrant testing simulator available for practice, and our Mobile training page explains delivery for local employers.

faq.q: What materials is liquid penetrant testing used on in Mobile?
faq.a: PT works on any non-porous material, including stainless steel, aluminum, nickel alloys, titanium and carbon steel. That makes it the natural choice for aluminum vessel structure and stainless chemical piping, where magnetic particles do not work.

faq.q: What kinds of defects can dye penetrant inspection find?
faq.a: Cracks, laps, seams and porosity that break the surface all show up as bleed-out. Flaws that stay buried cannot detect flaws below the surface, so volumetric concerns call for ultrasonic testing instead.

faq.q: What temperature limits apply to penetrant testing?
faq.a: The standard window in Article 6 of ASME Section V runs from 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit for part and materials alike. Beyond it the procedure needs qualification at the real temperature, which matters on sun-heated Mobile steel in summer.

faq.q: Does the penetrant used on stainless steel need to be special?
faq.a: Yes. Procedures for stainless and nickel alloys normally call for penetrant materials with controlled chlorine, fluorine and sulfur content, and the batch certifications are kept with the job records.

faq.q: Which codes cover PT acceptance for welds?
faq.a: ASME Section V Article 6 gives the method. Acceptance comes from the construction code, such as ASME B31.3 Table 341.3.2, ASME Section VIII Division 1 Appendix 8, or AWS D1.1 for structural steel. Your specification names the right one.

faq.q: Does Atlantis have staff in Mobile?
faq.a: No. Atlantis has no office in Mobile. Technicians travel to your shipyard, plant or fabrication shop for the agreed scope, and we coordinate access, permits and safety orientation with you beforehand.

faq.q: Can PT be performed on a ship in Mobile?
faq.a: Atlantis can examine welds and fittings on a vessel for the owner's own maintenance decisions. It holds no class-society approval, so any work that must be credited to a class survey needs a firm the society has approved.

faq.q: Why must surfaces be cleaned before penetrant testing?
faq.a: Oil, paint, scale, flux and grinding smear can block penetrant from entering a crack, hiding the very flaw you are looking for. Cleaning, and sometimes light etching, is therefore a required step in the procedure.

faq.q: How do I request a PT quote for a Mobile job?
faq.a: Send the material, component list, code, surface condition, site access notes and any restrictions on solvents or confined-space entry. With that information we can define the procedure and prepare the quotation.
